A.biggest_strength: Separating each iteration into a 'compare mid' step and a 'drop a half' step—with an explicit 'dropped' bracket, crossing low/high pointers on separate tracks, and a range ladder horizontally aligned with the array cells—makes the halving mechanism visually unmistakable.
A.biggest_weakness: Readers cannot click directly on an array cell to search for it, and the narrow phone view hides the text labels on the five scene buttons, leaving only numbered circles.

B.biggest_strength: Direct manipulation via clicking any cell in the 32-element array to search for it and dragging the log-scale array-size slider from 1 to 1,000,000,000 to compare linear vs. binary search counts.
B.biggest_weakness: Each step conflates the comparison with the range update, so the array simultaneously displays the old 'mid' alongside the already-shrunk '[lo, hi]' range (putting 'mid' outside '[lo, hi]' on every non-hit step and hiding 'lo' and 'hi' completely when 'lo > hi').

structured_output.reasons: Page A is the stronger explainer because its visual mechanics accurately and clearly show how binary search works: it separates comparing `mid` from dropping half the range, aligns its halving ladder directly with the 1D array cells (even on mobile), shows `low` crossing past `high` on a miss, and covers practical edge cases. Page B offers nice interactive touches (clickable cells and a continuous `n` slider), but collapsing compare-and-shrink into a single state causes `mid` to appear outside the active `[lo, hi]` range on every step and hides `lo`/`hi` when they cross, while its linear-scale halving ladder at n = 10^9 produces 21 visually identical 2px rows.
